Something is assailable when it has weaknesses or flaws that allow it to be attacked, challenged, or questioned — and those attacks have a reasonable chance of succeeding.

The root verb is assail, which means to attack something — not necessarily with fists, but with words, arguments, evidence, or criticism. When you add the suffix -able, you get a word that means capable of being assailed.

So if something is assailable, it means: there is a real opening to attack it, and that attack could land.
What kinds of things can be "assailable"?

This word is almost never used for physical things. It lives in the world of ideas, arguments, reputations, positions, and logic. Here are the typical targets:

  • An argument can be assailable if it has logical gaps or relies on shaky evidence.
  • A conclusion can be assailable if it doesn't follow cleanly from the facts.
  • A reputation can be assailable if there are past actions that critics can point to.
  • A claim can be assailable if someone can produce counter-evidence.
  • A legal position can be assailable if there are precedents or facts that work against it.
  • A theory can be assailable if it fails to account for certain known data.
The crucial nuance: "can be" vs. "has been"

Assailable means something is vulnerable to attack — not that it has already been attacked or destroyed. The word describes a potential, a weakness that exists, regardless of whether anyone has exploited it yet.

Think of it like a wall with a crack in it. The wall is assailable because the crack is there — whether or not anyone has pushed on it yet.

"The defendant's alibi was assailable — there were two hours in the evening that no witness could account for."

The alibi hasn't collapsed yet, but the weakness is there for a prosecutor to exploit.

You will almost certainly encounter the word unassailable far more often in English, because it is used much more frequently. Understanding the contrast sharpens your grasp of both words:

AssailableHas weaknesses; can be successfully attacked or challenged
UnassailableHas no weaknesses; impossible to successfully attack or challenge

"Her logic was unassailable — no one in the room could find a single flaw in it."

Flip it:

"His logic was assailable — the moment someone pointed out his flawed assumption, the whole argument fell apart."

When writers call something unassailable, they're making a very strong statement: try as hard as you like, you won't find a crack. Assailable is the acknowledgment that cracks exist.

Something can be more or less assailable. Writers often signal this with modifiers:

  • Easily assailable — very weak; almost anyone could poke holes in it.
  • Highly assailable — seriously flawed; a skilled critic would have no trouble dismantling it.
  • Somewhat assailable — has some weaknesses but isn't completely without merit.

"The report's methodology was somewhat assailable, but its core findings still held up."
Register: Where will you see this word?

Assailable is a formal, intellectual word. You'll find it most often in:

  • Academic writing (philosophy, law, science)
  • Legal arguments and courtroom language
  • Literary criticism and analysis
  • Formal journalism and opinion writing

You would rarely hear it in casual conversation. If you said "that's an assailable point" to a friend, they might not immediately know what you mean. In formal writing, however, it carries precise, clean meaning.
Two more examples to cement it

"The prosecutor argued that the eyewitness testimony was assailable — the witness had poor lighting conditions and admitted to being nervous."

Here, the testimony can be challenged because real, concrete weaknesses exist. The testimony isn't worthless, but it's not airtight either.

"Any political platform built on a single assumption is assailable; a good opponent only needs to disprove that one assumption to unravel the whole thing."

Here, assailable describes a structural vulnerability — one weak link that exposes the whole chain.
Assailable means: open to attack or challenge because of a real, identifiable weakness — the opposite of solid, airtight, or beyond question.
